1. ⚖️ Regulación

Regulatory and Supervisory Modernisation Principles: Consultation report

To remain effective, regulatory and supervisory frameworks must keep pace with the dynamic financial sector and be forward-looking and adaptive to current and future material risks. In this context, the FSB is proposing eight high-level principles for modernisation, addressed to financial authorities.

2. 🌪️ Clima & Catástrofes

Verisk estimates Isaias insured losses at $1-2bn, driven largely by wind damage

Verisk’s Catastrophe and Risk Solutions business has estimated insured industry losses to onshore property from Hurricane Isaias at between $1 billion and $2 billion, with wind damage expected to account for the vast majority of losses. Verisk explained that the estimate covers wind and privately insured storm surge losses from Isaias’ Florida Panhandle landfall. According to the firm, the most severe wind damage occurred west of Isaias’ landfall location, particularly in Florida’s Santa Rosa and northeastern Escambia counties.

  1. El contexto: Verisk explained that the estimate covers wind and privately insured storm surge losses from Isaias’ Florida Panhandle landfall.
  2. ¿Por qué importa? Impacto directo en exposición, pricing y reservas del sector.
  3. ¿Qué vigilar? El sector deberá revisar modelos de pricing y cobertura en las zonas afectadas ante el incremento de eventos extremos.

Verisk estimates Hurricane Isaias insured onshore property losses in $1bn to $2bn range

Verisk, a catastrophe risk modelling and data analytics specialist, has now issued an initial industry insured loss estimate for recent hurricane Isaias, saying that onshore property losses from the storm could reach $2 billion. Verisk’s initial industry loss estimate includes losses from wind and privately insured storm surge, as a result of hurricane Isaias’ landfall in the Florida Panhandle. Cotality (formerly CoreLogic), estimated that insured losses from wind and storm surge from hurricane Isaias will be in the $2 billion to $3 billion range.

5. 🌪️ Clima & Catástrofes

Mid-single-digit billions of dollars loss from Isaias unlikely to affect P&C re/insurer credit profiles, says Fitch

A wide rage of insurers and reinsurers are expected to be impacted by Hurricane Isaias, which made landfall as a Category 2 storm in the Florida Panhandle on October 9th, but while the event is expected to drive moderate economic and insured losses, Fitch says it is “not likely to affect credit for rated property/casualty (P/C) (re)insurers.” Hurricane Isaias peaked as a Category 3 major hurricane over the Gulf before increasing wind shear weakened it on approach, eventually making landfall as a Category 2 storm with maximum sustained winds of 105 mph, although has now been downgraded to a tropical storm. In affected areas like Florida, Alabama, Georgia, and The Carolinas, Fitch expects the storm to result in moderate economic and insured losses, estimating that industry losses could reach the mid-single-digit billions of dollars. “The storm’s reduced intensity at landfall is expected to result in more manageable insured losses,” says Fitch.

  1. El contexto: In affected areas like Florida, Alabama, Georgia, and The Carolinas, Fitch expects the storm to result in moderate economic and insured losses, estimating that industry losses could reach the mid-sing.

PICC P&C’s new $12m Great Wall Re is the first Hong Kong sidecar ILS issuance

PICC Property and Casualty Company Limited has now reported that its new US $12 million issuance of insurance-linked securities under its Great Wall Re Limited special purpose insurer is actually a quota share reinsurance sidecar, the first in Hong Kong, designed to provide protection to its offshore wind power property insurance book on the Chinese Mainland. This morning PICC Property and Casualty Company has said that the US $12 million (HK $94m) Great Wall Re ILS issuance is “the first issuance of insurance-linked securities with a “sidecar” structure in the Hong Kong market,” and the first issuance of sidecar insurance-linked securities by any domestic Chinese insurance company. The insurer said this is “another innovative practice for the company to use the international capital market to spread insurance risks after the successful issuance of disaster bonds in Hong Kong in 2022.” Being a sidecar, the underlying subject reinsurance arrangement with this US $12 million Great Wall Re deal is a quota share, or proportional reinsurance, transferring the risks to capital market investors on that basis.

In the current, very competitive reinsurance operating landscape, the importance of stability and consistency have been key, but the executive emphasised that consistency doesn’t mean doing the same things, but “keeping a very open dialogue, working with an open solution mindset, and finding ways to deliver to clients.” In terms of what makes a really productive insurer and reinsurer relationship, da Victoria Lobo highlighted dialogue, depth, and delivery. This was the message from Nikhil da Victoria Lobo, Head of P&C for Western & Southern Europe and the Middle East & Africa at global reinsurer Swiss Re, in a video interview with Reinsurance News ahead of the annual Baden-Baden meeting . As the global reinsurance industry heads to Baden-Baden, the January renewals will of course be a big topic, and against a backdrop of a complex and increasingly interconnected risk landscape, dialogue, depth, and delivery are key to a productive insurer and reinsurer relationship.

Hurricane Simon track remained outside of Mexico cat bond parametric trigger zones: Loconte

As major hurricane Simon’s path shifted west it appears to have remained offshore of the important parametric trigger zones related to the $175 million IBRD CAR Mexico 2024 (Pacific) catastrophe bond, according to analysis by Isacco Loconte an insurance-linked securities (ILS) Investment Specialist at asset manager Azimut Switzerland SA. As we had been reporting over the weekend , hurricane Simon’s minimum central pressure, a critical factor in determining whether any payout would come due for the catastrophe bond, did deepen to a sufficiently low level to activate a payout should the storm’s track have crossed into any of the parametric trigger boxes. While those pressure levels were strong enough to meet the L1 payout threshold for the parametric zones, the hurricane trajectory worked in the bond’s favor.” Based on the parametric trigger design, hurricane Simon’s central pressure would have needed to be at 932mb or lower to activate a payout from the zones it came closest to.

Carrier Management · 28 Sep · 1 min General

AI Fuels 440% Surge in Hackers Using Blockchains in Attacks

Open-source artificial intelligence is making it easier for hackers to hide malicious code on blockchains, opening a new front in a crypto industry already grappling with rising cybercrime. In the attacks documented by the report, hackers use a blockchain to leave instructions for that software, such as the location of the server that controls it, a technique known as a “blockchain dead drop.” This can make an attack harder to stop because information recorded on a blockchain cannot be easily removed. Blockchains are typically not involved in the initial infection of a machine, which often happens through conventional means such as supply-chain attacks or malicious downloads, Eric Jardine, head of research at Chainalysis, said in response to questions over email.

Reinsurance rate declines may slow by 2028, soft market floor may not be found till 2030: Jefferies

Analysts from Jefferies are not confident that reinsurance leadership teams are fully-acknowledging how fast rates have been softening and believe that the focus will shift to terms and conditions from 2028, while a soft market floor may not be found until 2030. From 2028, when the expected slow-down in rate softening occurs, the Jefferies team expect that, “Thereafter, we expect softening to be on the terms and conditions, which tend to deteriorate late in a cycle, once reinsurers can no longer afford to give up premium income.” Adding that, “We eventually expect prices and terms to find a floor in 2030.” Pricing is deteriorating faster than management teams had expected, the Jefferies team believe, with third-party capital seen as one factor. “In our view, the pace of decline will accelerate next year, and only start to slow in 2028.” In a similar fashion to the softening of the reinsurance market, particularly in US property catastrophe risks, through the 2010’s, the Jefferies team expect that once reinsurers begin to appreciate just how much the reduction in pricing is affecting their premium income, the focus will shift towards a quickening of the relaxation of terms and conditions.
